nodes.chainStep: Cardiac monitor and vitals; look for hypotension or shock, altered mental status, chest pain or acute heart failure; a 12-lead ECG during the tachycardia before any drug, never delaying a shock for instability
nodes.why: A 12-lead ECG during the tachycardia is recommended for every stable patient, and documenting the rhythm on it is the step everything else depends on; with the history and examination it names the cause in up to a third of patients with palpitations. Instability is checked at the same time: hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, acute heart failure or signs of shock. A drug comes after the rhythm is recorded, a troponin and an x-ray do not name it, and ambulatory monitoring is for palpitations the 12-lead did not catch.

nodes.summary: No pulse, or polymorphic VT that will not stop: defibrillate and run cardiac arrest care, which is outside this pathway. Sustained torsades that does not stop gets an immediate shock, then magnesium as in the torsades route.

Bradycardia with shock: IV atropine, then temporary pacing if it fails, transcutaneous as the emergency bridge and transvenous when available, with labs for a reversible cause (potassium, calcium, pH, digoxin level, thyroid function, Lyme titer). This pathway hands off here; the syncope pathway's unstable bradycardia route carries the sources, and the atropine dose is still pending there.

nodes.ask: A tachyarrhythmia, not sinus, is causing shock or ischemia. Next?
options: Synchronized cardioversion now, with sedation if awake

Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes, then reassess
nodes.chainStep: Synchronized DC cardioversion now, with sedation if conscious; an unsynchronized shock if synchronization is not possible; in AF, start anticoagulation as soon as possible without delaying the shock
nodes.why: A tachyarrhythmia that is causing hemodynamic instability is cardioverted at once. Synchronized cardioversion is recommended for unstable narrow and wide QRS tachycardias, DC cardioversion is first-line for monomorphic VT that is not tolerated, and immediate electrical cardioversion is recommended when AF, pre-excited AF included, is the cause. The shock is synchronized to the QRS to avoid inducing VF, or unsynchronized if synchronization is not possible. In AF, anticoagulation starts as soon as possible around an unscheduled cardioversion, without holding up an immediate shock. Rate control or an antiarrhythmic infusion first is for the stable patient.

nodes.ask: Stable, regular narrow-complex tachycardia. First treatment?
options: Modified Valsalva: strain, then lie flat with legs raised

IV verapamil now, with IV metoprolol if it is slow to work
nodes.chainStep: Modified Valsalva: strain semi-recumbent for about 15 seconds (blow into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to move the plunger), then straight to supine with the legs raised; carotid sinus massage only on one side, for no more than 5 seconds
nodes.why: Vagal maneuvers come first in a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, preferably supine with the legs raised, and the adenosine and diltiazem labels ask for them before the drug. The modified Valsalva, a semi-recumbent strain followed at once by lying flat with a passive leg raise, converted 43% against 17% for the standard strain, and a network meta-analysis ranked it the most effective vagal maneuver, ahead of carotid sinus massage. Carotid massage is only ever one side, for at most 5 seconds, and avoided after a TIA or stroke or with a carotid bruit. An IV calcium channel blocker and an IV beta blocker are not given within a few hours of each other.

nodes.chainStep: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV bolus over 1 to 2 seconds, close to the patient, with a rapid saline flush; 12 mg if no conversion in 1 to 2 minutes, repeated once; record the ECG during the push
nodes.why: Adenosine is the drug once a vagal maneuver fails. It works only as a rapid bolus, given over 1 to 2 seconds as close to the patient as possible and chased with a rapid saline flush; 12 mg follows if 6 mg has not stopped it within 1 to 2 minutes, and the US label allows that 12 mg once more. It does not convert flutter, AF or VT, though the brief AV block can show flutter waves. In a stable patient the sequence after adenosine is a calcium channel blocker or beta blocker, and cardioversion when drugs fail.

The calcium channel blockers are avoided with hypotension or a reduced EF, and IV beta blockers with decompensated heart failure. An IV calcium channel blocker and an IV beta blocker are not given within a few hours of each other: fatal cardiac arrests have followed esmolol with IV verapamil. Synchronized cardioversion follows when drug therapy fails.

nodes.chainStep: Look for a medical driver (sepsis, bleeding, PE, heart failure, ACS) and treat it first; echo or a known LVEF; CBC, metabolic panel and thyroid function; pin down the time of onset
nodes.why: First decide whether the AF is primary or a response to illness. Sepsis, bleeding, PE, heart failure or ACS can drive a fast rate; then the cause is treated aggressively, cardioversion may be harmful and aggressive rate control is avoided. New AF gets an echo, a CBC, metabolic panel and thyroid function, but not protocolized testing for ischemia, ACS or PE unless something points to them. The LVEF chooses the rate-control drug, and the time of onset decides whether early cardioversion is safe.

nodes.summary: AF driven by sepsis, bleeding or PE: treat the cause first; cardioversion may be harmful and aggressive rate control is avoided. Continue in the sepsis and fever, GI bleed or dyspnea pathway. With thyrotoxicosis, a beta blocker eases the symptoms and the rate while antithyroid treatment restores a euthyroid state, after which the AF usually resolves; anticoagulation follows the stroke risk score until thyroid function is normal and sinus rhythm holds. In sepsis the benefit of anticoagulation during the critical illness is uncertain; stroke prevention is decided afterwards by the risk score.

nodes.chainStep: Rate control with an IV beta blocker and/or digoxin (0.25 to 0.5 mg IV, then 0.25 mg every 4 to 6 hours to 1.5 mg in 24 hours); no IV diltiazem or verapamil; IV amiodarone if these fail or cannot be used
nodes.why: With moderate or severe LV systolic dysfunction, IV diltiazem and verapamil are Class 3: Harm, so the calcium channel blockers are kept for an EF over 40%; beta blockers and/or digoxin are the rate-control drugs at an EF of 40% or less, and IV amiodarone is the option when they fail or cannot be used. Ibutilide is best avoided at an EF of 40% or less because torsades is more frequent, and flecainide is not given with structural heart disease, HFrEF included. With a reduced EF and persistent AF, a trial of rhythm control is recommended to see whether the AF is contributing, once anticoagulation allows it.

nodes.chainStep: Rate control, or rhythm control now: synchronized electrical cardioversion under sedation (150 to 200 J for AF, 100 J or less for flutter), or IV ibutilide (EF over 40%, ECG monitoring for 4 hours), procainamide or amiodarone; anticoagulation around it by onset and stroke risk; waiting up to 48 hours for spontaneous conversion is also acceptable
nodes.why: With a clear onset under 48 hours, the US guideline does not require 3 weeks of anticoagulation first, so rate control and early cardioversion are both open; ESC adds that waiting up to 48 hours for spontaneous conversion is reasonable. Whatever the duration, 3 weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation meets the US requirement before an elective cardioversion. Electrical cardioversion is the more effective, when sedation is acceptable. Ibutilide usually works within 30 to 90 minutes and converts flutter more often than AF, but needs ECG monitoring for 4 hours after the infusion because of torsades; IV amiodarone is reasonable but slow, 8 to 12 hours, and procainamide is an alternative. A single-dose flecainide pill in the pocket is reasonable only after it has been tested in a monitored setting, and IV diltiazem rarely converts AF or flutter.

nodes.ask: The rate has settled. Long-term stroke prevention?
options: Score stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) and anticoagulate by it

nodes.chainStep: Score CHA2DS2-VASc: anticoagulate at 2 or more in men, 3 or more in women (a DOAC over warfarin unless moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve); reasonable at 1 in men, 2 in women; none at 0 in men, 1 in women; find and modify bleeding risk factors
nodes.why: Long-term anticoagulation follows the stroke risk score, whatever the pattern of AF and whether or not sinus rhythm has returned. A CHA2DS2-VASc of 2 or more in men or 3 or more in women means anticoagulation, a DOAC in preference to warfarin; 1 in men or 2 in women makes it reasonable. Flutter is scored the same way. Aspirin is not an alternative, and a bleeding score identifies risks to modify, not who is denied anticoagulation. ESC 2024 uses CHA2DS2-VA, dropping sex: 2 or more recommends anticoagulation, and 1 means consider it.

nodes.summary: High stroke risk: long-term anticoagulation, a DOAC over warfarin unless there is a mechanical valve or moderate to severe mitral stenosis; aspirin is not a substitute. Rate or rhythm control continues, with cardiology follow-up.

Intermediate stroke risk: anticoagulation is reasonable (US) and should be considered at a CHA2DS2-VA of 1 (ESC), decided with the patient; after any cardioversion it continues at least 4 weeks regardless.

Low stroke risk: no long-term anticoagulation, and aspirin adds nothing. After a cardioversion the US rule is still at least 4 weeks of anticoagulation, though its benefit is uncertain under 12 hours at this score. ESC 2024 makes it optional only with no risk factors and sinus rhythm within 24 hours of onset.

A stable patient gets IV ibutilide or IV procainamide as the alternative to elective cardioversion, an unstable one electrical cardioversion, and catheter ablation of the pathway follows.

nodes.why: When the mechanism of a wide QRS tachycardia is not fully understood, it is treated as VT, and prompt termination is recommended even when it is tolerated, because deterioration can be sudden. ESC makes synchronized cardioversion first-line for tolerated monomorphic VT when the sedation risk is low, with IV procainamide (IIa, structural heart disease included) or IV amiodarone (IIb) as the drugs; the US procainamide label covers sustained VT. Verapamil and diltiazem are contraindicated: given in VT, they have caused hemodynamic deterioration and VF. Adenosine or vagal maneuvers are considered only when SVT is likely and there is no pre-excitation.

nodes.why: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV is the first-line drug for torsades whatever the serum magnesium, repeated if episodes persist, together with removal of the offending drug and potassium supplementation (to 4.5 to 5 mmol/L, IIb in the US statement). If torsades recurs despite that, raising the heart rate with isoproterenol or transvenous pacing above 70 per minute suppresses it. Procainamide, a class 1A drug, is contraindicated in torsades; amiodarone prolongs the QT and can itself cause torsades, and QT-prolonging drugs such as sotalol are avoided. A run that does not stop, or degenerates into VF, gets an immediate shock.

nodes.chainStep: IV calcium first for ECG changes (calcium gluconate 1 g in the US consensus; 6.8 mmol in the UK guideline), repeated if no effect in 5 to 10 minutes; then insulin with glucose (UK: 10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose) and nebulized albuterol (UK: 10 to 20 mg); remove potassium (dialysis or a binder); cardiac monitoring; glucose checks for up to 12 hours
nodes.why: ECG changes mean the heart is at risk, so IV calcium comes first: it improves the ECG within about 3 minutes but does not lower the potassium, and the dose is repeated if there is no effect in 5 to 10 minutes. Then potassium is shifted into cells with insulin and glucose plus nebulized albuterol (not albuterol alone in severe hyperkalemia), and removed, by dialysis in a patient on hemodialysis. Bicarbonate is not routine, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not recommended in the acute setting.

nodes.chainStep: Find and treat the cause: bleeding or dehydration, infection or fever, PE, anemia, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, pain or anxiety, and drugs (beta-agonists, methylxanthines, beta-blocker withdrawal); the rate itself is not the target
nodes.why: Sinus tachycardia is a response, treated by finding and removing its cause: anxiety, anemia, fever, dehydration, infection, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, PE, myocardial infarction, heart failure or shock, and drugs such as beta-agonists, methylxanthines, cocaine or amphetamines, or beta-blocker withdrawal. Slowing the rate is not the aim; the short-acting beta blocker esmolol is labeled only for a noncompensatory sinus tachycardia that needs specific treatment. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is diagnosed only after these causes are excluded.

nodes.summary: Sinus tachycardia with features of PE: continue in the dyspnea pathway, where PE is weighed by clinical probability. The tachycardia is a response, not the target.
Sinus tachycardia from sepsis: continue in the sepsis and fever pathway. The rate settles as the infection and the circulation are treated; it is not slowed with drugs.
Sinus tachycardia from bleeding: resuscitate and continue in the GI bleed pathway. The tachycardia is compensation; the treatment is the bleeding.
Sinus tachycardia from a drug or stimulant: remove or treat the cause; poisoning continues in the toxic ingestion pathway, alcohol withdrawal in the altered mental status pathway.

Thyrotoxicosis: a beta blocker for the symptoms and the tachycardia (propranolol also slows T4 to T3 conversion), and antithyroid treatment with endocrinology; if AF develops, anticoagulate by stroke risk until thyroid function is normal and sinus rhythm holds. Thyroid storm continues in the altered mental status pathway.

Sinus tachycardia with no cause found: home with follow-up. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a diagnosis of exclusion; a 24-hour Holter mean over 90 with waking rates over 100 supports it, and reassurance, exercise training, volume expansion and avoiding stimulants come before any drug.

nodes.chainStep: Red flags: structural heart disease, a family history of sudden cardiac death or an inherited channelopathy, syncope with the palpitations; if they persist or stay unexplained, an ambulatory ECG by frequency: a 24 to 48 hour Holter for daily palpitations, a patient-activated loop or event recorder (about 2 weeks) for infrequent ones; a symptom diary
nodes.why: A normal 12-lead between episodes does not exclude an arrhythmia: history, examination and the ECG make the diagnosis in up to a third, and ambulatory monitoring is the tool for the rest. Most palpitations are benign; monitoring is indicated when the story suggests an arrhythmia, when the patient needs reassurance and an explanation, and specifically with structural heart disease, a family history of sudden cardiac death or an inherited channelopathy. After an unexplained sudden death under 50 in the family, the evaluation includes ECG, echocardiography and exercise testing. The device follows the frequency: a 24 to 48 hour Holter for daily palpitations, a loop or event recorder for infrequent, unpredictable ones, where about 2 weeks gives the best yield for the cost, with a diary of the episodes.

cases.label: Pre-excitation on the resting ECG
cases.vignette: 22-year-old woman, three episodes this year of a sudden racing heartbeat that stopped as suddenly; well now. BP 116/72, HR 74.

results.front: Monitor: sinus rhythm 74. BP 116/72.
results.ecg: 12-lead: sinus rhythm 74, short PR interval, a slurred upstroke to the QRS (delta wave), QRS 120 ms; QTc 420 ms.

cases.label: Sinus tachycardia after cocaine
cases.vignette: 27-year-old man, palpitations and jitteriness at 2 a.m. after a night out; he used cocaine 2 hours ago. BP 152/94, HR 126, no chest pain.

results.front: Monitor: sinus tachycardia at 126. BP 152/94, alert, agitated.
results.ecg: 12-lead: sinus tachycardia at 126, no ST changes.
results.sinus_cause: Dilated pupils, sweaty, no chest pain. Temperature 37.6. Hemoglobin and TSH normal.
